content.content:
# The law file

An agent writes a database call into a page component. The build stays green. The law is the file `.lawcheck/law.yaml`. In it, you say which kinds of files the repository has, and which rules the files of each kind keep. Under a law whose page components may not use the database code, Lawcheck reports that call as `forbidden-use`.

Lawcheck looks for the file in the current directory, then in each directory above it. The nearest directory that holds it is the root of the law. Lawcheck runs git and the script rules in the root. Every path of the law starts there. When the root lies below the top of the git work tree, Lawcheck judges only the files below the root. A law past 1 MiB, 10,000 rules or 1,000 types, subtypes included, stops the run with `file-too-large`.

## Keys

| Key | In | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `lawcheck` | top | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, required |
| `required` | top | patterns of files that must have a type |
| `ignored` | top | patterns of files that the law leaves out |
| `rules` | top | rule id to rule |
| `types` | top | type id to root type |
| `why` | rule | one line, required |
| `status` | rule | `enforced` or `advisory` |
| `context` | rule | paths |
| `companion` | rule | a path |
| `about` | type | one line |
| `paths` | type | patterns, required |
| `content` | type | a regular expression |
| `rules` | type | rule ids |
| `may_use` | type | type ids |
| `types` | type | type id to subtype |
| `waivers` | type | `true` or `false` |

Lawcheck stops with `law-invalid` in these cases:

- a key outside the table;
- a key written twice;
- an empty file;
- a value of the wrong kind.

When a key outside the table differs by one or two letters from a known key, the `law-invalid` message ends with a hint that names the known key, such as `(did you mean 'paths'?)`.

A YAML alias, such as `*base`, stands for the value that an anchor, such as `&base`, marks. Lawcheck reads an alias as the value of its anchor.

Lawcheck stops with `law-invalid` when a type holds itself through an alias. For example, a subtype `again: *source` under `source: &source` makes `source` hold itself.

The law below uses every key of the table except `required`, `ignored`, `context`, `companion`, `may_use` and `waivers`:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  no-console:
    why: Only the command layer writes to the terminal.
  no-todo:
    why: A TODO without an issue number gets forgotten.
    status: advisory

types:
  source:
    about: Everything that ships.
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.d.ts"]
    rules: [no-todo]
    types:
      library:
        about: Code the commands call.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
        rules: [no-console]
      command:
        about: The command layer.
        paths: ["src/cli/**"]
  script:
    about: Executable helpers.
    paths: ["tools/**/*.{mjs,js}"]
    content: "^#!"
    rules: [no-todo]
```

## lawcheck

`lawcheck` holds the version of the law's format, in the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, such as `0.1.0`. Lawcheck checks only that form, and it does not compare the value with its own version. `lawcheck init` writes the format of the Lawcheck that runs it: `0.1.0` for every 0.1.0 release, alpha versions included.

## required

`required` lists the patterns of the files that must have a type. The section "Patterns" below gives their syntax. A text file that git lists, that a pattern of `required` matches and that no type takes is the finding `untyped-file`. With `required: ["src/**"]`, a file that an agent adds in a new folder `src/gen/` fails the check until a type takes it.

With `required: ["src/**"]` and a type whose `paths` take only `src/**/*.ts`, a stylesheet or an empty placeholder file in `src/` is also `untyped-file`. A `!` pattern leaves such files out of `required`, as in `required: ["src/**", "!src/**/*.css"]`.

`untyped-file` is an error in the change and a warning in debt, like `forbidden-use`. A binary file, a symbolic link and a file under `ignored` are never `untyped-file`. Without `required`, a file that no type takes is no finding.

A non-empty `required` needs at least one pattern without `!`. A wrong pattern is `law-invalid`.

## ignored

`ignored` lists the patterns of the files that the law leaves out. A file that a pattern of `ignored` matches has no type, even when the paths of a type match it. No rule judges it, its waivers are not read, and it is never `untyped-file`. A use of such a file is a use of a file with no type, so a `may_use` list in force forbids it.

`ignored` suits generated code inside a folder under `required`, such as `ignored: ["src/gen/**"]`. A non-empty `ignored` needs at least one pattern without `!`.

## rules

`rules` maps each rule id to its rule. Each rule has one file in `.lawcheck/rules/` (section "Rule files" below). Lawcheck judges no file against a rule that no type lists. For such a rule, `lawcheck explain --rule <id>` says so.

### why

`why` is one line of at most 200 characters. Every rule needs it. Lawcheck prints it under each finding of the rule. Each prompt that Lawcheck sends for a reviewer rule holds it.

### status

`status` is `enforced`, the default, or `advisory`. A finding of an enforced rule in the change (lawcheck docs concepts) is an error, which makes the run exit 1. A finding of an advisory rule is a warning, which leaves the exit code at 0.

### context

`context` is a list of paths from the root, for a reviewer rule alone. On a script rule, `context` is `law-invalid`. Each path names a file that git lists and that is not binary. The reviewer gets each of these files with every file it judges for the rule (`lawcheck docs reviewer-rules`).

### companion

`companion` is the path of an ES module in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`, for a reviewer rule alone. On a script rule, `companion` is `law-invalid`, and so is a path outside that folder, a path that git does not list, and a binary file. For each file that the rule judges, the module returns the paths of the files that go into that file's prompt, after the files of `context`. With `companion: .lawcheck/rules/lib/spec-of-test.mjs`, a rule can send each test with the spec it covers (`lawcheck docs reviewer-rules`).

## types

`types` maps each type id to its type.

### about

`about` is one line that describes the type. `lawcheck explain` and `lawcheck prime` print it.

### paths

`paths` lists the patterns of the type's files. Every type needs it. At least one of its patterns must have no `!`. The section "Patterns" below gives their syntax.

### content

`content` is a JavaScript regular expression with the flag `m`. A file that matches `paths` takes the type only when the expression matches a part of its text. An expression that JavaScript cannot compile is `law-invalid`. The message gives JavaScript's own words.

### rules

`rules` lists the ids of the rules that the type's files keep. Each id must be a rule of the law. An id listed twice counts once.

### may_use

`may_use` lists the types whose files this type's files may use (lawcheck docs concepts). A type without the key takes the list of the nearest type above it that has one. That list is the list in force for the type. With no list on the type or above it, a file of the type may use any file. Lawcheck then reads none of its uses.

A list in force works this way:

- it allows a target whose type is a listed type or a subtype of one;
- a type may use its own files only when its list names it;
- `may_use: []` allows no use;
- no list allows a use of a file that has no type;
- each id of the list must be a type of the law.

Lawcheck does not judge a use of a binary file, nor a file's use of itself. It reports each use that the list does not allow as the finding `forbidden-use`. `lawcheck docs languages` lists, for each language, the forms of a use that Lawcheck reads.

### types

`types` holds the subtypes of the type, with the same keys (section "The type of a file" below).

### waivers

With `waivers: false`, Lawcheck reads a waiver marker in the type's files as plain text. That way, a documentation page or a test whose text quotes the marker can have a type and waive nothing. Without the key, a type takes the value of its parent. In a type at the top of `types` without the key, Lawcheck reads waivers.

## Ids

A rule id and a type id are kebab-case: lower-case letters and digits, in words joined by `-`. The pattern is `[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*`. Each type id may appear once in the whole tree of types. A key that YAML reads as no string, such as `true` or `12`, is `law-invalid`. Write such a key in quotes.

A rule id may not equal a code of Lawcheck (`lawcheck docs codes` lists the codes). The reserved ids include `forbidden-use`, `uses-not-read`, `untyped-file`, `parser-failed` and `already-initialized`.

## Patterns

A pattern matches the whole path from the root. A segment is the part of a path between two `/`, or before the first or after the last. A pattern tells upper case from lower case on every system.

- `*` matches any run of characters without `/`, the empty run included. `?` matches one such character. A leading dot in a name is a character like any other: `*` matches `.env`.
- `**` is a whole segment. Before the last segment, it matches any number of directories, none included. As the last segment, it matches every file below its directory at any depth. It does not match the path of the directory itself.
- `{a,b}` matches one of its alternatives. An alternative is not empty. It holds no `/`, `{`, `}` or `,`, and it may hold `*` and `?`.
- Every other character matches itself. A pattern has no escape character.
- A leading `!` makes the pattern an exclusion. A file matches a list when it matches one plain pattern and no exclusion. The order of the list does not matter.

Lawcheck refuses these patterns with `law-invalid`:

- an empty pattern, or a pattern with an empty segment;
- a segment `.` or `..`;
- `**` beside other characters in one segment;
- `!` alone;
- a brace that is nested, unclosed or unopened, or that holds a `/` or an empty alternative.

## The type of a file

Lawcheck takes the regular files that `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` lists at the root. These listed files have no type:

- a symbolic link;
- a file that git does not track and `.gitignore` names;
- `.lawcheck/verdicts` and `.lawcheck/.gitattributes`;
- a binary file, which Lawcheck tells by a byte of value 0 in its first 8,000 bytes;
- a file that a pattern of `ignored` matches.

Lawcheck judges a file like any other when its name holds a line break, a carriage return, a backslash or bytes that are not UTF-8. It prints such a name with `\n`, `\r`, `\\` and `\xHH` in their place.

A submodule is a git repository held inside another one. Lawcheck judges no file of a submodule, or of another repository inside this one. It prints a note when the paths of a type reach into one.

Lawcheck tests a file against the types at the top of `types`, `paths` first and then `content`. It then tests the file against the subtypes of the type that matched, one level at a time. The deepest match is the type of the file. The rules of every type on the way down bind the file, each rule once. No rule judges a file that no type matches. Under `required`, such a file is the finding `untyped-file`.

When two types of one level both match a file, every run stops with `type-overlap` and exit 2. To split two types by path, add a `!` pattern to one of them. To give some files of a type a type of their own by their text, make a subtype with a `content` expression under that type (Types for an existing project (lawcheck docs types-for-a-project)). A second type of the same level with the same `paths` and a `content` overlaps the first, because the first type matches every file that the second one matches. `lawcheck explain <path>` shows how a file got its type.

## Rule files

Each rule has one file in `.lawcheck/rules/`:

- `<id>.mjs` for a script rule (`lawcheck docs script-rules`);
- `<id>.md` for a reviewer rule (`lawcheck docs reviewer-rules`).

Lawcheck stops with exit 2 and one of two codes when the rule files do not match the law:

- `rule-missing-file`, for a rule with neither file, or with a reviewer file that holds only whitespace;
- `rule-file-without-entry`, for a rule with both files, and for any other file in `.lawcheck/rules/` outside `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`.

A script rule keeps the code it imports in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`, and the companion of a reviewer rule lies there too. Lawcheck sees only the files that git lists, so a rule file that git does not track and `.gitignore` names counts as missing.

Next: Settings (lawcheck docs config)
# Types for an existing project

You end with a law whose types (lawcheck docs concepts) cover the folders of an existing project. No file falls in two types, and one type of the law takes its files by their text, through a `content` expression. For any path, `lawcheck explain` prints its type and the reason.

The outputs below come from a repository with `scripts/release.mjs` and five files under `src/`:

- `src/api/orders.ts`;
- `src/core/price.ts`;
- `src/core/price.test.ts`, which tests `src/core/price.ts`;
- `src/db/orders.ts`;
- `src/generated/schema.ts`, which a code generator writes.

Its top folder is the root (lawcheck docs concepts) of the law: you ran `lawcheck init` there (The first type and the first rule (lawcheck docs first-law)).

## 1. See the files without a type

```text
$ lawcheck explain .
```

```output
./  8 files
  no type  8 files
```

`explain` with a folder counts the files git lists below it, by type. The two files `init` wrote count too.

## 2. Describe the folders as types

Give each folder of `src/` a type. A type under the `types` key of another type is a subtype. Lawcheck tests a subtype on a file only after the file matched its parent. Under the parent `source`, `api` takes the `.ts` files of `src/api/` and no other file. Write this into `.lawcheck/law.yaml`:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

types:
  source:
    about: Everything that ships.
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts"]
    types:
      api:
        about: The HTTP handlers.
        paths: ["src/api/**"]
      core:
        about: The business logic.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
      db:
        about: The database access.
        paths: ["src/db/**"]
  script:
    about: The release scripts.
    paths: ["scripts/**"]
```

## 3. See the files of each type

```text
$ lawcheck explain .
```

```output
./  8 files
  source  1 file
  api  1 file
  core  2 files
  db  1 file
  script  1 file
  no type  2 files
```

The file of `source` is `src/generated/schema.ts`. It matches `src/**/*.ts` and no subtype. The two files without a type are the files of `.lawcheck/`. No rule judges a file without a type.

## 4. See why a file has its type

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/api/orders.ts
```

```output
src/api/orders.ts
  type:  api  (source > api)  The HTTP handlers.
  matched:  source by "src/**/*.ts", api by "src/api/**"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  waivers:  none
```

The `type` line gives the chain from the top-level type down to the type of the file: `source > api`. The `matched` line gives the pattern that matched at each level. The rules of every type in the chain bind (lawcheck docs concepts) the file.

## 5. List the files of one type

```text
$ lawcheck explain --type core
```

```output
type core  (source > core)  The business logic.
  paths:  src/core/**
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  subtypes:  none
  files:  2
    src/core/price.test.ts
    src/core/price.ts
```

`core` holds the test of `src/core/price.ts` too. The next step gives the tests a type, because they need rules of their own.

## 6. Add a type for the tests

Add these lines at the end of `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, under `types`, beside `source` and `script`:

```yaml
  test:
    about: The tests.
    paths: ["src/**/*.test.ts"]
```

## 7. Run a check

```text
$ lawcheck check
```

```output
lawcheck: ERROR  1 error

src/core/price.test.ts  error[type-overlap]  the file matches the types 'source' and 'test' of one level
  why:  a file has one type, so the rules that bind it are never in doubt

next: narrow the paths or content of the types that overlap in .lawcheck/law.yaml, then run lawcheck check
```

`src/core/price.test.ts` matches the two top-level types `source` and `test`. A file has one type. Every run stops with exit 2 until one of the two types leaves the file out (type-overlap (lawcheck docs codes)).

## 8. Leave the tests out of source

A pattern that starts with `!` excludes the files it matches. Give `source` these `paths`:

```yaml
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts"]
```

## 9. See the type of the test

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/core/price.test.ts
```

```output
src/core/price.test.ts
  type:  test  (test)  The tests.
  matched:  test by "src/**/*.test.ts"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  waivers:  none
```

## 10. Leave the generated file out

The code generator writes `src/generated/schema.ts` again on every build, so a fix by hand in that file lasts until the next build. Leave the file out of the law with a second exclusion in the `paths` of `source`:

```yaml
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts", "!src/generated/**"]
```

## 11. See the generated file

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/generated/schema.ts
```

```output
src/generated/schema.ts
  type:  none: no type's paths match it, so no rule judges it
```

## 12. See the type of a file you have not written yet

`explain` takes a path that does not exist. It answers with the law a new file there would get:

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/api/refunds.ts
```

```output
src/api/refunds.ts  (does not exist yet)
  type:  api  (source > api)  The HTTP handlers.
  matched:  source by "src/**/*.ts", api by "src/api/**"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
```

## 13. Write a test beside the code

A test can sit beside the code, under a name that no pattern tells apart from the code. Write one such test, `src/core/rounding.ts`:

```ts
import { test } from 'node:test';
import { price } from './price';

test('a price is a whole number', () => price);
```

## 14. Give the tests beside the code a type by their text

With a `content` expression, a type takes only the files whose text matches it. Put such a type under the type that takes the file by its paths, because Lawcheck tests a subtype only on the files that matched its parent. In `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, replace the three lines of `core` with these:

```yaml
      core:
        about: The business logic.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
        types:
          core-test:
            about: The tests beside the business logic.
            paths: ["src/core/**"]
            content: "from 'node:test'"
```

If you put the type with `content` beside `core`, every run stops with `type-overlap`. Both types of that level match the test, because `core` takes it by its paths alone.

```

src/core/rounding.ts
  type:  core-test  (source > core > core-test)  The tests beside the business logic.
  matched:  source by "src/**/*.ts", core by "src/core/**", core-test by "src/core/**" and content "from 'node:test'"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  waivers:  none
```

The `matched` line names the pattern and the content that gave the file the type `core-test`. `src/core/price.ts` holds no `from 'node:test'`. It keeps the type `core`.

The law file (lawcheck docs law) describes every key of a type and every form of a pattern.

toolUseResult.stdout:
# The law file

An agent writes a database call into a page component. The build stays green. The law is the file `.lawcheck/law.yaml`. In it, you say which kinds of files the repository has, and which rules the files of each kind keep. Under a law whose page components may not use the database code, Lawcheck reports that call as `forbidden-use`.

Lawcheck looks for the file in the current directory, then in each directory above it. The nearest directory that holds it is the root of the law. Lawcheck runs git and the script rules in the root. Every path of the law starts there. When the root lies below the top of the git work tree, Lawcheck judges only the files below the root. A law past 1 MiB, 10,000 rules or 1,000 types, subtypes included, stops the run with `file-too-large`.

## Keys

| Key | In | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `lawcheck` | top | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, required |
| `required` | top | patterns of files that must have a type |
| `ignored` | top | patterns of files that the law leaves out |
| `rules` | top | rule id to rule |
| `types` | top | type id to root type |
| `why` | rule | one line, required |
| `status` | rule | `enforced` or `advisory` |
| `context` | rule | paths |
| `companion` | rule | a path |
| `about` | type | one line |
| `paths` | type | patterns, required |
| `content` | type | a regular expression |
| `rules` | type | rule ids |
| `may_use` | type | type ids |
| `types` | type | type id to subtype |
| `waivers` | type | `true` or `false` |

Lawcheck stops with `law-invalid` in these cases:

- a key outside the table;
- a key written twice;
- an empty file;
- a value of the wrong kind.

When a key outside the table differs by one or two letters from a known key, the `law-invalid` message ends with a hint that names the known key, such as `(did you mean 'paths'?)`.

A YAML alias, such as `*base`, stands for the value that an anchor, such as `&base`, marks. Lawcheck reads an alias as the value of its anchor.

Lawcheck stops with `law-invalid` when a type holds itself through an alias. For example, a subtype `again: *source` under `source: &source` makes `source` hold itself.

The law below uses every key of the table except `required`, `ignored`, `context`, `companion`, `may_use` and `waivers`:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  no-console:
    why: Only the command layer writes to the terminal.
  no-todo:
    why: A TODO without an issue number gets forgotten.
    status: advisory

types:
  source:
    about: Everything that ships.
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.d.ts"]
    rules: [no-todo]
    types:
      library:
        about: Code the commands call.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
        rules: [no-console]
      command:
        about: The command layer.
        paths: ["src/cli/**"]
  script:
    about: Executable helpers.
    paths: ["tools/**/*.{mjs,js}"]
    content: "^#!"
    rules: [no-todo]
```

## lawcheck

`lawcheck` holds the version of the law's format, in the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, such as `0.1.0`. Lawcheck checks only that form, and it does not compare the value with its own version. `lawcheck init` writes the format of the Lawcheck that runs it: `0.1.0` for every 0.1.0 release, alpha versions included.

## required

`required` lists the patterns of the files that must have a type. The section "Patterns" below gives their syntax. A text file that git lists, that a pattern of `required` matches and that no type takes is the finding `untyped-file`. With `required: ["src/**"]`, a file that an agent adds in a new folder `src/gen/` fails the check until a type takes it.

With `required: ["src/**"]` and a type whose `paths` take only `src/**/*.ts`, a stylesheet or an empty placeholder file in `src/` is also `untyped-file`. A `!` pattern leaves such files out of `required`, as in `required: ["src/**", "!src/**/*.css"]`.

`untyped-file` is an error in the change and a warning in debt, like `forbidden-use`. A binary file, a symbolic link and a file under `ignored` are never `untyped-file`. Without `required`, a file that no type takes is no finding.

A non-empty `required` needs at least one pattern without `!`. A wrong pattern is `law-invalid`.

## ignored

`ignored` lists the patterns of the files that the law leaves out. A file that a pattern of `ignored` matches has no type, even when the paths of a type match it. No rule judges it, its waivers are not read, and it is never `untyped-file`. A use of such a file is a use of a file with no type, so a `may_use` list in force forbids it.

`ignored` suits generated code inside a folder under `required`, such as `ignored: ["src/gen/**"]`. A non-empty `ignored` needs at least one pattern without `!`.

## rules

`rules` maps each rule id to its rule. Each rule has one file in `.lawcheck/rules/` (section "Rule files" below). Lawcheck judges no file against a rule that no type lists. For such a rule, `lawcheck explain --rule <id>` says so.

### why

`why` is one line of at most 200 characters. Every rule needs it. Lawcheck prints it under each finding of the rule. Each prompt that Lawcheck sends for a reviewer rule holds it.

### status

`status` is `enforced`, the default, or `advisory`. A finding of an enforced rule in the change (lawcheck docs concepts) is an error, which makes the run exit 1. A finding of an advisory rule is a warning, which leaves the exit code at 0.

### context

`context` is a list of paths from the root, for a reviewer rule alone. On a script rule, `context` is `law-invalid`. Each path names a file that git lists and that is not binary. The reviewer gets each of these files with every file it judges for the rule (`lawcheck docs reviewer-rules`).

### companion

`companion` is the path of an ES module in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`, for a reviewer rule alone. On a script rule, `companion` is `law-invalid`, and so is a path outside that folder, a path that git does not list, and a binary file. For each file that the rule judges, the module returns the paths of the files that go into that file's prompt, after the files of `context`. With `companion: .lawcheck/rules/lib/spec-of-test.mjs`, a rule can send each test with the spec it covers (`lawcheck docs reviewer-rules`).

## types

`types` maps each type id to its type.

### about

`about` is one line that describes the type. `lawcheck explain` and `lawcheck prime` print it.

### paths

`paths` lists the patterns of the type's files. Every type needs it. At least one of its patterns must have no `!`. The section "Patterns" below gives their syntax.

### content

`content` is a JavaScript regular expression with the flag `m`. A file that matches `paths` takes the type only when the expression matches a part of its text. An expression that JavaScript cannot compile is `law-invalid`. The message gives JavaScript's own words.

### rules

`rules` lists the ids of the rules that the type's files keep. Each id must be a rule of the law. An id listed twice counts once.

### may_use

`may_use` lists the types whose files this type's files may use (lawcheck docs concepts). A type without the key takes the list of the nearest type above it that has one. That list is the list in force for the type. With no list on the type or above it, a file of the type may use any file. Lawcheck then reads none of its uses.

A list in force works this way:

- it allows a target whose type is a listed type or a subtype of one;
- a type may use its own files only when its list names it;
- `may_use: []` allows no use;
- no list allows a use of a file that has no type;
- each id of the list must be a type of the law.

Lawcheck does not judge a use of a binary file, nor a file's use of itself. It reports each use that the list does not allow as the finding `forbidden-use`. `lawcheck docs languages` lists, for each language, the forms of a use that Lawcheck reads.

### types

`types` holds the subtypes of the type, with the same keys (section "The type of a file" below).

### waivers

With `waivers: false`, Lawcheck reads a waiver marker in the type's files as plain text. That way, a documentation page or a test whose text quotes the marker can have a type and waive nothing. Without the key, a type takes the value of its parent. In a type at the top of `types` without the key, Lawcheck reads waivers.

## Ids

A rule id and a type id are kebab-case: lower-case letters and digits, in words joined by `-`. The pattern is `[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*`. Each type id may appear once in the whole tree of types. A key that YAML reads as no string, such as `true` or `12`, is `law-invalid`. Write such a key in quotes.

A rule id may not equal a code of Lawcheck (`lawcheck docs codes` lists the codes). The reserved ids include `forbidden-use`, `uses-not-read`, `untyped-file`, `parser-failed` and `already-initialized`.

## Patterns

A pattern matches the whole path from the root. A segment is the part of a path between two `/`, or before the first or after the last. A pattern tells upper case from lower case on every system.

- `*` matches any run of characters without `/`, the empty run included. `?` matches one such character. A leading dot in a name is a character like any other: `*` matches `.env`.
- `**` is a whole segment. Before the last segment, it matches any number of directories, none included. As the last segment, it matches every file below its directory at any depth. It does not match the path of the directory itself.
- `{a,b}` matches one of its alternatives. An alternative is not empty. It holds no `/`, `{`, `}` or `,`, and it may hold `*` and `?`.
- Every other character matches itself. A pattern has no escape character.
- A leading `!` makes the pattern an exclusion. A file matches a list when it matches one plain pattern and no exclusion. The order of the list does not matter.

Lawcheck refuses these patterns with `law-invalid`:

- an empty pattern, or a pattern with an empty segment;
- a segment `.` or `..`;
- `**` beside other characters in one segment;
- `!` alone;
- a brace that is nested, unclosed or unopened, or that holds a `/` or an empty alternative.

## The type of a file

Lawcheck takes the regular files that `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` lists at the root. These listed files have no type:

- a symbolic link;
- a file that git does not track and `.gitignore` names;
- `.lawcheck/verdicts` and `.lawcheck/.gitattributes`;
- a binary file, which Lawcheck tells by a byte of value 0 in its first 8,000 bytes;
- a file that a pattern of `ignored` matches.

Lawcheck judges a file like any other when its name holds a line break, a carriage return, a backslash or bytes that are not UTF-8. It prints such a name with `\n`, `\r`, `\\` and `\xHH` in their place.

A submodule is a git repository held inside another one. Lawcheck judges no file of a submodule, or of another repository inside this one. It prints a note when the paths of a type reach into one.

Lawcheck tests a file against the types at the top of `types`, `paths` first and then `content`. It then tests the file against the subtypes of the type that matched, one level at a time. The deepest match is the type of the file. The rules of every type on the way down bind the file, each rule once. No rule judges a file that no type matches. Under `required`, such a file is the finding `untyped-file`.

When two types of one level both match a file, every run stops with `type-overlap` and exit 2. To split two types by path, add a `!` pattern to one of them. To give some files of a type a type of their own by their text, make a subtype with a `content` expression under that type (Types for an existing project (lawcheck docs types-for-a-project)). A second type of the same level with the same `paths` and a `content` overlaps the first, because the first type matches every file that the second one matches. `lawcheck explain <path>` shows how a file got its type.

## Rule files

Each rule has one file in `.lawcheck/rules/`:

- `<id>.mjs` for a script rule (`lawcheck docs script-rules`);
- `<id>.md` for a reviewer rule (`lawcheck docs reviewer-rules`).

Lawcheck stops with exit 2 and one of two codes when the rule files do not match the law:

- `rule-missing-file`, for a rule with neither file, or with a reviewer file that holds only whitespace;
- `rule-file-without-entry`, for a rule with both files, and for any other file in `.lawcheck/rules/` outside `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`.

A script rule keeps the code it imports in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`, and the companion of a reviewer rule lies there too. Lawcheck sees only the files that git lists, so a rule file that git does not track and `.gitignore` names counts as missing.

Next: Settings (lawcheck docs config)
# Types for an existing project

You end with a law whose types (lawcheck docs concepts) cover the folders of an existing project. No file falls in two types, and one type of the law takes its files by their text, through a `content` expression. For any path, `lawcheck explain` prints its type and the reason.

The outputs below come from a repository with `scripts/release.mjs` and five files under `src/`:

- `src/api/orders.ts`;
- `src/core/price.ts`;
- `src/core/price.test.ts`, which tests `src/core/price.ts`;
- `src/db/orders.ts`;
- `src/generated/schema.ts`, which a code generator writes.

Its top folder is the root (lawcheck docs concepts) of the law: you ran `lawcheck init` there (The first type and the first rule (lawcheck docs first-law)).

## 1. See the files without a type

```text
$ lawcheck explain .
```

```output
./  8 files
  no type  8 files
```

`explain` with a folder counts the files git lists below it, by type. The two files `init` wrote count too.

## 2. Describe the folders as types

Give each folder of `src/` a type. A type under the `types` key of another type is a subtype. Lawcheck tests a subtype on a file only after the file matched its parent. Under the parent `source`, `api` takes the `.ts` files of `src/api/` and no other file. Write this into `.lawcheck/law.yaml`:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

types:
  source:
    about: Everything that ships.
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts"]
    types:
      api:
        about: The HTTP handlers.
        paths: ["src/api/**"]
      core:
        about: The business logic.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
      db:
        about: The database access.
        paths: ["src/db/**"]
  script:
    about: The release scripts.
    paths: ["scripts/**"]
```

## 3. See the files of each type

```text
$ lawcheck explain .
```

```output
./  8 files
  source  1 file
  api  1 file
  core  2 files
  db  1 file
  script  1 file
  no type  2 files
```

The file of `source` is `src/generated/schema.ts`. It matches `src/**/*.ts` and no subtype. The two files without a type are the files of `.lawcheck/`. No rule judges a file without a type.

## 4. See why a file has its type

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/api/orders.ts
```

```output
src/api/orders.ts
  type:  api  (source > api)  The HTTP handlers.
  matched:  source by "src/**/*.ts", api by "src/api/**"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  waivers:  none
```

The `type` line gives the chain from the top-level type down to the type of the file: `source > api`. The `matched` line gives the pattern that matched at each level. The rules of every type in the chain bind (lawcheck docs concepts) the file.

## 5. List the files of one type

```text
$ lawcheck explain --type core
```

```output
type core  (source > core)  The business logic.
  paths:  src/core/**
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  subtypes:  none
  files:  2
    src/core/price.test.ts
    src/core/price.ts
```

`core` holds the test of `src/core/price.ts` too. The next step gives the tests a type, because they need rules of their own.

## 6. Add a type for the tests

Add these lines at the end of `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, under `types`, beside `source` and `script`:

```yaml
  test:
    about: The tests.
    paths: ["src/**/*.test.ts"]
```

## 7. Run a check

```text
$ lawcheck check
```

```output
lawcheck: ERROR  1 error

src/core/price.test.ts  error[type-overlap]  the file matches the types 'source' and 'test' of one level
  why:  a file has one type, so the rules that bind it are never in doubt

next: narrow the paths or content of the types that overlap in .lawcheck/law.yaml, then run lawcheck check
```

`src/core/price.test.ts` matches the two top-level types `source` and `test`. A file has one type. Every run stops with exit 2 until one of the two types leaves the file out (type-overlap (lawcheck docs codes)).

## 8. Leave the tests out of source

A pattern that starts with `!` excludes the files it matches. Give `source` these `paths`:

```yaml
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts"]
```

## 9. See the type of the test

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/core/price.test.ts
```

```output
src/core/price.test.ts
  type:  test  (test)  The tests.
  matched:  test by "src/**/*.test.ts"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  waivers:  none
```

## 10. Leave the generated file out

The code generator writes `src/generated/schema.ts` again on every build, so a fix by hand in that file lasts until the next build. Leave the file out of the law with a second exclusion in the `paths` of `source`:

```yaml
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts", "!src/generated/**"]
```

## 11. See the generated file

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/generated/schema.ts
```

```output
src/generated/schema.ts
  type:  none: no type's paths match it, so no rule judges it
```

## 12. See the type of a file you have not written yet

`explain` takes a path that does not exist. It answers with the law a new file there would get:

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/api/refunds.ts
```

```output
src/api/refunds.ts  (does not exist yet)
  type:  api  (source > api)  The HTTP handlers.
  matched:  source by "src/**/*.ts", api by "src/api/**"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
```

## 13. Write a test beside the code

A test can sit beside the code, under a name that no pattern tells apart from the code. Write one such test, `src/core/rounding.ts`:

```ts
import { test } from 'node:test';
import { price } from './price';

test('a price is a whole number', () => price);
```

## 14. Give the tests beside the code a type by their text

With a `content` expression, a type takes only the files whose text matches it. Put such a type under the type that takes the file by its paths, because Lawcheck tests a subtype only on the files that matched its parent. In `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, replace the three lines of `core` with these:

```yaml

        about: The business logic.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
        types:
          core-test:
            about: The tests beside the business logic.
            paths: ["src/core/**"]
            content: "from 'node:test'"
```

If you put the type with `content` beside `core`, every run stops with `type-overlap`. Both types of that level match the test, because `core` takes it by its paths alone.

```text
$ lawcheck explain src/core/rounding.ts
```

```output
src/core/rounding.ts
  type:  core-test  (source > core > core-test)  The tests beside the business logic.
  matched:  source by "src/**/*.ts", core by "src/core/**", core-test by "src/core/**" and content "from 'node:test'"
  may use:  any file; no type on the way up has may_use
  rules:  none
  waivers:  none
```

The `matched` line names the pattern and the content that gave the file the type `core-test`. `src/core/price.ts` holds no `from 'node:test'`. It keeps the type `core`.

The law file (lawcheck docs law) describes every key of a type and every form of a pattern.
